cards.statement: Google's DR guide describes the cold pattern as one with spare recovery resources already in place before a disaster.
cards.explanation: In the cold pattern no spare resources are on hand, so recovery must first obtain them, and the service stays down until they arrive.
cards.misconception: The cold DR pattern keeps spare recovery resources provisioned before a disaster.

cards.statement: Google's DR guide associates tighter recovery targets with higher application running costs.
cards.explanation: Tighter RTO and RPO targets often require more replication, capacity, and operational complexity, increasing the application's running cost.

cards.statement: A warm disaster recovery design keeps the application serving traffic throughout recovery.
cards.explanation: Warm DR includes an interruption while recovery resources are made ready. Prepared standby components reduce setup work, but the application still needs recovery time.
cards.misconception: Warm recovery keeps the application continuously available during recovery.

cards.statement: Google recommends an internal availability SLO that is stricter than the external SLA commitment.
cards.explanation: A stricter internal availability SLO warns the team early enough to address reliability problems before breaching the external SLA commitment.

cards.statement: Compute Engine resource-based commitments can follow a workload when it moves between regions.
cards.explanation: A resource-based Compute Engine commitment covers eligible usage in the region where it was purchased. Its regional scope stays fixed when a workload moves.
cards.misconception: A resource-based commitment transfers its discount coverage to another region with the workload.

source.title: Committed use discounts for Compute Engine

cards.statement: Compute flexible committed use discounts can reserve VM capacity for the committed workload.
cards.explanation: Compute flexible commitments don't support attached reservations and come with no assured capacity, so a workload that needs assured VM capacity uses a separate reservation.
cards.misconception: Purchasing a compute flexible commitment also secures the workload's VM capacity.

source.title: Combine reservations with committed use discounts

cards.statement: Pub/Sub lets billing and audit services receive the same events through independent subscriptions.
cards.explanation: Pub/Sub delivers a topic's events independently to its subscriptions, so each business consumer processes its own copy.

cards.statement: Apigee can expose a JSON API to consumers while the backend continues to exchange XML messages.
cards.explanation: Apigee's mediation policies translate payloads at the API facade, allowing a legacy XML backend to serve JSON clients.

cards.statement: DORA groups failed deployment recovery time with deployment frequency as a software delivery throughput factor.
cards.explanation: DORA measures throughput with change lead time, deployment frequency and failed deployment recovery time; change fail rate and deployment rework rate measure instability.

cards.statement: The Well-Architected Framework recommends shedding excess requests at the frontend during overload.
cards.explanation: The reliability pillar recommends shedding excess requests at the frontend so overload does less damage to backend components.

cards.statement: The regional deployment archetype automatically fails over applications to another region during a region outage.
cards.explanation: A regional deployment uses zones within one region. A region outage causes downtime, so recovery in another region needs a separately planned deployment or restore.
cards.misconception: A regional architecture includes recovery from a whole-region outage.

cards.statement: For a regional MIG spread across three zones, Google recommends overprovisioning the group by at least 50%.
cards.explanation: Losing one of three zones removes a third of capacity, so Google recommends at least 50% extra instances, and doubling for two zones, so the remaining zones carry the full load.

cards.statement: Cloud SQL high availability places its standby instance in a different region from the primary.
cards.explanation: Cloud SQL high availability places the primary and standby in different zones of the same region. This protects against a zonal failure.
cards.misconception: Cloud SQL high availability provides a cross-region standby.

cards.statement: Spanner automatically moves leaders to another read-write region when a multi-region leader region fails.
cards.explanation: If a multi-region configuration's default leader region becomes unavailable, Spanner places its database leaders in the second read-write region.

cards.statement: Standard Tier prioritizes keeping outbound traffic on Google's backbone until it reaches an edge near the user.
cards.explanation: Standard Tier normally exits Google's network near the resource's region. Peering or transit networks carry traffic onward to the internet user.
cards.misconception: Standard Tier prioritizes a long outbound path across Google's global network.

cards.statement: Enabling Cloud CDN caching on a load balancer requires that load balancer to use Network Service Tiers' Premium Tier.
cards.explanation: Cloud CDN is always Premium Tier and can't be used with Standard Tier, so choosing Standard Tier to lower a load balancer's egress cost rules out Cloud CDN caching.

cards.statement: A Project Owner can manually delete a backup vault's backups before their enforced retention ends.
cards.explanation: Enforced retention makes a vault's backups immutable: no user, including a Project Owner, and not even Google can manually delete them until the retention period has passed.
cards.misconception: Project Owner permissions override a backup vault's enforced retention.

source.title: Backup vaults for immutable and indelible backups

cards.statement: An app's session files in a Cloud Run instance's local filesystem carry over to its replacement instance.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run loses files in the instance's local writable filesystem when that instance stops. Session data needing persistence belongs in external storage.
cards.misconception: Cloud Run carries instance-local session files into replacement instances.

cards.statement: Each Shared VPC service project in an organization attaches to a single host project at any given time.
cards.explanation: A host project can share subnets with many service projects, but each service project can be attached to only one host project, so it uses that one host's Shared VPC network.

cards.statement: A Private Service Connect endpoint lets consumers access producer VM subnets through private network routes.
cards.explanation: Private Service Connect endpoints expose a published service IP with NAT to its load balancer. They provide service access rather than general VPC connectivity.
cards.misconception: A Private Service Connect endpoint opens routed access to the producer's VM network.

cards.statement: By default, an external proxy Network Load Balancer passes client source IPs and ports through to its backends.
cards.explanation: By default the target proxy drops the original client IP and port, so backends see the proxy as the source. Enabling the PROXY protocol on the target proxy preserves that client information.
cards.misconception: A proxy Network Load Balancer hands each client's source IP to backends with no extra configuration.

source.title: External proxy Network Load Balancer overview

cards.statement: Dataflow lets a team reuse Apache Beam transforms across its batch and streaming pipelines.
cards.explanation: Dataflow uses Apache Beam's shared programming model for batch and streaming, allowing teams to reuse processing logic across those workloads.

cards.statement: Bigtable supports multi-row atomic transactions for applications that update related records together.
cards.explanation: Bigtable's atomic transaction boundary is a single row. An application that needs related changes across rows as one transaction needs another database design.
cards.misconception: Bigtable can commit several related rows as one atomic transaction.

cards.statement: Firestore's Android client synchronizes offline document updates by default when connectivity returns.
cards.explanation: Firestore's Android client enables offline persistence by default and syncs local document changes to the backend when the device reconnects.

cards.statement: Cloud Run supports privileged containers for applications that need host-level device access.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run excludes privileged containers from its runtime contract. Applications that depend on privileged execution need a different compute design.
cards.misconception: Cloud Run accepts privileged containers for host-dependent applications.

cards.statement: Compute Engine extended memory adds RAM to supported custom VMs while leaving the vCPU count unchanged.
cards.explanation: Supported Compute Engine custom machine series offer extended memory, letting memory-heavy workloads add RAM beyond the default ratio for their vCPU count.

source.title: Create a VM with a custom machine type

cards.statement: Cloud Interconnect encrypts traffic by default for an on-premises link carrying sensitive data.
cards.explanation: Cloud Interconnect traffic uses no encryption by default. A design that needs encrypted transport adds an encryption mechanism.
cards.misconception: Cloud Interconnect's private physical path supplies encryption by default.

cards.statement: Migration Center can assess PostgreSQL databases as part of a Google Cloud migration inventory.
cards.explanation: Migration Center accepts PostgreSQL inventory and performance data for assessment, helping architects include database requirements in migration planning.

cards.statement: Migration Center derives network dependency reports from vSphere scans of the source environment.
cards.explanation: Migration Center collects network connection evidence through the discovery client's OS scans. A vSphere scan does not supply that evidence.
cards.misconception: Hypervisor discovery alone supplies the connection evidence needed for network dependency planning.

source.title: Generate and analyze network dependencies report

cards.statement: One Migration Center TCO report can compare several migration preference sets for one asset group.
cards.explanation: When generating a TCO report, a team picks asset groups and assigns each group multiple preference sets, so one report compares migration scenarios side by side.

cards.statement: Rehosting a workload on Google Cloud gives it horizontal scalability as part of the migration itself.
cards.explanation: Rehost moves workloads with minor or no changes, so Google notes they aren't optimized for the cloud afterwards and miss features such as horizontal scalability; replatform or refactor work adds that.
cards.misconception: A lift-and-shift migration leaves workloads optimized for the cloud.

source.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started

cards.statement: Google classifies replacing on-premises collaboration software with Google Workspace as a repurchase migration.
cards.explanation: Repurchase means moving from a purchased on-premises workload to a cloud-hosted SaaS equivalent, rather than moving its code or rebuilding it.

source.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started

cards.statement: License Mobility through Software Assurance lets architects bring Windows Server licenses to Compute Engine.
cards.explanation: Windows Server's operating-system license falls outside License Mobility through Software Assurance. Google documents separate eligibility checks for other BYOL rights.
cards.misconception: License Mobility through Software Assurance covers the Windows Server operating system.
cards.volatilityNote: Software licensing eligibility depends on Microsoft's current terms.

source.title: Microsoft licensing on Google Cloud FAQ

cards.statement: Google recommends first-mover workloads with few dependencies for teams new to Google Cloud migrations.
cards.explanation: Google's first-mover guidance favors few dependencies so teams learn migration patterns before coordinating complex workload groups.

source.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Assess and discover your workloads

cards.statement: The Well-Architected Framework recommends frequent small changes with fast feedback to accommodate change.
cards.explanation: The framework's design-for-change principle favors incremental delivery and rapid feedback so teams can keep adjusting their architecture.

cards.statement: Cloud DNS shortens existing resolver cache entries when an architect lowers a record's TTL before migration.
cards.explanation: A lower Cloud DNS TTL takes effect after the previous cached value expires. Plan that wait before the migration cutover.
cards.misconception: Changing the authoritative TTL immediately shortens the lifetime of records already cached by resolvers.

cards.statement: HA VPN requires a BGP-capable peer gateway when an architect connects an on-premises network.
cards.explanation: HA VPN uses dynamic BGP routing, so the on-premises VPN gateway needs BGP capability for route exchange.

cards.statement: HA VPN qualifies for an availability SLA when a single gateway interface carries its tunnels.
cards.explanation: An HA VPN gateway with one active interface has no availability SLA. The topology needs redundancy across its interfaces to qualify.
cards.misconception: One active HA VPN gateway interface provides an availability SLA.
cards.volatilityNote: Google can change the topologies that qualify for an HA VPN availability SLA.

cards.statement: Cloud Router automatically manages route exchange while Google's VPC infrastructure forwards application packets.
cards.explanation: Cloud Router operates in the control plane through BGP sessions. Google's Andromeda infrastructure performs packet forwarding.

cards.statement: Google's Partner Interconnect SLA covers the segment between the provider network and the VPC network.
cards.explanation: Google's Partner Interconnect SLA covers the Google-to-provider connection. Coverage for the provider-to-customer segment depends on the provider.
cards.volatilityNote: Google or a connectivity provider can change the scope of contractual availability coverage.

cards.statement: Network Connectivity Center lets a VPC spoke exclude selected subnet ranges from export to its hub.
cards.explanation: Network Connectivity Center provides VPC spoke export filters. Excluding subnet ranges limits which routes that spoke shares with the hub.

cards.statement: VPC Network Peering lets two networks exchange subnet traffic through a mutually peered third network.
cards.explanation: VPC Network Peering connects adjacent peers rather than providing transitive routing. Two networks sharing a peer need another connectivity path between them.
cards.misconception: A shared VPC peer acts as a transit network between its other peers.

cards.statement: Cloud IDS automatically blocks a network flow when its inspection engine detects an intrusion.
cards.explanation: Cloud IDS inspects mirrored traffic and alerts on threats. Enforcement needs a separate control because Cloud IDS takes no action to block an attack.
cards.misconception: Cloud IDS combines threat detection with automatic blocking of the original traffic.

cards.statement: A Cloud Armor policy on a Cloud Run service's load balancer also protects its direct service URL.
cards.explanation: Cloud Armor evaluates requests through the protected load balancer. A client reaching Cloud Run's default URL bypasses that policy, so the design needs ingress restrictions.
cards.misconception: Cloud Armor protection at the load balancer extends to direct Cloud Run URL requests.

cards.statement: Cloud NAT lets a VM accept internet connections initiated by outside clients through the NAT gateway.
cards.explanation: Cloud NAT translates outbound connections and their response traffic. It rejects unsolicited inbound connections, so a public listener needs a different ingress design.
cards.misconception: Cloud NAT's shared external addresses expose VMs to client-initiated inbound connections.

cards.statement: Autoclass automatically promotes a colder Cloud Storage object to Standard storage when an app reads it.
cards.explanation: Autoclass moves an object's data back to Standard storage after a read, so renewed access changes the storage class used for future accesses.

cards.statement: Cloud Storage soft delete can recover an overwritten object as a new live version during its retention period.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage keeps overwritten objects in a soft-deleted state for the retention period. Restoring one creates a new live copy in the same bucket.

cards.statement: Local SSD automatically replicates workload data to preserve it after an unrecoverable host failure.
cards.explanation: Local SSD is attached to the VM's physical host and lacks automatic replication. Host errors can lose its data, so durable recovery needs another copy.
cards.misconception: Local SSD automatically replicates data for durable recovery after host failure.

cards.statement: Compute Engine standard snapshots share unchanged disk blocks by default across a disk's snapshot chain.
cards.explanation: After the first full snapshot, later standard snapshots normally store changed data and reference existing blocks. Compute Engine sometimes captures a fresh full image.

source.title: About archive and standard disk snapshots

cards.statement: Cloud SQL can use its high availability standby to serve application read queries while the primary is healthy.
cards.explanation: A Cloud SQL high availability standby reserves its role for failover rather than serving read queries. A read replica is the design for offloading reads.
cards.misconception: The high availability standby doubles as a read-serving instance while the primary is healthy.

cards.statement: Spanner requires the Enterprise Plus edition for a database with a multi-region instance configuration.
cards.explanation: Spanner places multi-region instance configurations in Enterprise Plus. Selecting that deployment scope therefore affects the edition an architect chooses.
cards.volatilityNote: Google can change the instance configurations included in each Spanner edition.

cards.statement: Bigtable multi-cluster routing provides immediate read-your-writes consistency across replicas by default.
cards.explanation: Bigtable multi-cluster routing offers eventual consistency. A read routed to another cluster may miss a just-completed write while replication catches up.
cards.misconception: Multi-cluster routing makes an acknowledged write immediately visible in each replicated cluster.

cards.statement: BigQuery's secondary dataset replica accepts independent application writes in its own region.
cards.explanation: A BigQuery secondary dataset replica is read-only until promoted to primary. Application writes go to the primary replica.
cards.misconception: A secondary BigQuery dataset replica accepts independent writes alongside the primary.

cards.statement: BigQuery's pre-run cost estimate for a query on a clustered table can exceed the bytes the query finally scans.
cards.explanation: BigQuery learns which clustered blocks it can skip only during execution, so the estimate before a run isn't exact and the final cost reflects the blocks scanned. Partitioning gives granular pre-run estimates.

cards.statement: Compute Engine's autoscaler automatically combines scaling signals using the largest suggested VM count.
cards.explanation: The autoscaler derives a VM count from each scaling signal and selects the largest. This lets a workload scale for whichever bottleneck demands more instances.

source.title: Using an autoscaling policy with multiple signals

cards.statement: Managed instance group autohealing restores application health by rerouting requests to healthy VMs.
cards.explanation: Autohealing recreates VMs whose applications fail the configured health check. Load balancing redirects requests away from unhealthy VMs.
cards.misconception: Autohealing repairs an application by redirecting its traffic rather than recreating its VM.

source.title: Set up an application-based health check and autohealing

cards.statement: Compute Engine's default sole-tenant maintenance policy live-migrates VMs within a fixed server pool.
cards.explanation: Compute Engine's Default sole-tenant maintenance policy lets eligible VMs migrate to new physical servers. Migrate within node group confines migration to a fixed server pool.
cards.misconception: The default sole-tenant maintenance policy preserves the fixed physical-server pool needed by some licenses.

cards.statement: GKE keeps a regional cluster's control plane available for management during a single-zone outage.
cards.explanation: GKE places regional control plane replicas in different zones of one region, preserving access to the Kubernetes API during a zone outage.

cards.statement: A team running GKE Standard creates a separate Autopilot cluster to put some workloads on Autopilot-managed nodes.
cards.explanation: Autopilot ComputeClasses let a Standard cluster run selected workloads on Autopilot-managed node pools alongside the team's own Standard node pools, in the same cluster.
cards.misconception: Autopilot-managed workloads need their own Autopilot cluster when a team also runs Standard node pools.

source.title: About Autopilot mode workloads in GKE Standard

cards.statement: A fleet supports GKE clusters from different projects under a shared fleet host project.
cards.explanation: The fleet host project holds the fleet resource, while registered clusters can remain in other projects. This enables management across project boundaries.

cards.statement: VMware Engine gives the default vCenter user full administrator access to vCenter in a private cloud.
cards.explanation: VMware Engine keeps full administrative access to a private cloud; its default vCenter user, CloudOwner, gets Cloud-Owner-Role privileges, enough to deploy and manage VMs.
cards.misconception: The default vCenter user holds full vCenter administrator rights.

cards.statement: VM Manager bases patch compliance on reported OS inventory and the OS distribution's update metadata.
cards.explanation: VM Manager periodically compares VM inventory with distribution update metadata; its dashboard reflects that reported patch state.

cards.statement: Agent Platform Pipelines runs Kubeflow Pipelines SDK workflows on Google-managed infrastructure.
cards.explanation: Agent Platform Pipelines runs compatible Kubeflow Pipelines SDK workflows as a managed service. Google operates the execution infrastructure, reducing the team's cluster-management work.
cards.volatilityNote: Supported pipeline execution features can evolve as Agent Platform changes.

source.title: Introduction to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines

cards.statement: Agent Platform Pipelines runs tasks with independent inputs sequentially by default within a pipeline run.
cards.explanation: Agent Platform Pipelines runs independent tasks in parallel by default. The workflow DAG's input-output dependencies impose ordering when one task consumes another task's output.
cards.misconception: The order in a pipeline definition forces independent tasks to execute serially.
cards.volatilityNote: Pipeline scheduling defaults and workflow capabilities may change.

source.title: Introduction to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines

cards.statement: Agent Platform ML Metadata traces a model back to the datasets and runs that produced it.
cards.explanation: Agent Platform ML Metadata records links between artifacts and executions. The lineage graph supports auditing which training data and workflow runs contributed to a model.
tags: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform ML Metadata
cards.volatilityNote: Agent Platform's metadata and lineage capabilities may evolve.

source.title: Introduction to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform ML Metadata

cards.statement: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Model Garden can offer managed APIs or self-deployment for selected open models.
cards.explanation: Model Garden offers managed APIs for selected open models and self-deployment into your Google Cloud project. A model's available serving options determine who provisions its serving infrastructure.
tags: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Model Garden
cards.volatilityNote: Model Garden's model catalog and available serving options change over time.

source.title: Deploy open models from Model Garden

cards.statement: Cluster Director gives AI Hypercomputer GPU clusters a managed Slurm environment, so teams skip installing Slurm.
cards.explanation: For a managed Slurm experience Google points to Cluster Director, while Cluster Toolkit deploys blueprints that install Slurm on clusters the team runs itself.

source.title: Plan and create your AI infrastructure

cards.statement: Compute Engine fulfills a Flex-start MIG resize request incrementally as individual GPUs become available.
cards.explanation: Compute Engine fulfills a Flex-start MIG resize request by creating the VM group together after requested capacity becomes available. This suits training jobs that need their workers at the same time.
cards.misconception: A Flex-start MIG resize request grows its worker group gradually as individual GPUs become available.
cards.volatilityNote: GPU consumption options and provisioning guarantees may change.

source.title: About resize requests in a MIG

cards.statement: Cloud Vision API SafeSearch can score hateful imagery as a separate moderation category.
cards.explanation: Cloud Vision API SafeSearch scores adult, spoof, medical, violence, and racy content. Its categories exclude hate-content classification, so moderation designs need a separate capability for that risk.
cards.misconception: SafeSearch covers hate-content detection as part of its explicit-content classification.
cards.volatilityNote: SafeSearch's available moderation categories may evolve.

cards.statement: Gemini Enterprise uses project IAM grants to override source-document ACLs for ACL-enabled connectors.
cards.explanation: Gemini Enterprise uses your identity provider to check whether the end user can access each document a connector returns; IAM roles on the project grant no extra document access.
cards.misconception: Project IAM roles replace source-document permissions when a third-party connector enforces ACLs.

cards.statement: Gemini Notebook Enterprise can automatically refresh imported Google Docs used for answer grounding.
cards.explanation: Gemini Notebook Enterprise creates a static copy of imported sources for analysis. Its answers use that copy, so a later edit to the original Google Doc does not change the imported content.
cards.misconception: Imported Google Docs remain live-linked for automatic grounding in subsequent document edits.
cards.volatilityNote: Source ingestion and grounding behavior may change as Gemini Notebook Enterprise evolves.

cards.statement: When an administrator destroys a Cloud KMS key version, Cloud KMS erases its key material right away.
cards.explanation: Destroying a key version puts it in the scheduled-for-destruction state, 30 days by default and configurable at key creation, and it can be restored during that time.
cards.misconception: Scheduling a key version for destruction destroys its key material immediately.

cards.statement: Organization policy constraints can block service account key creation even when IAM permits that operation.
cards.explanation: An enforced service account key creation constraint prevents key creation even for principals with the corresponding IAM permission. This provides a guardrail across affected projects.

source.title: Best practices for using service accounts securely

cards.statement: Cloud KMS Admin includes ciphertext decryption permission for direct calls to the Cloud KMS API.
cards.explanation: Cloud KMS Admin lacks direct decryption permission. Key management and direct cryptographic use need separate grants, supporting separation of duties.
cards.misconception: Cloud KMS Admin includes direct decryption permission alongside key administration.

cards.statement: Cloud EKM's external key manager can revoke a Google Cloud project's permission to use an encryption key.
cards.explanation: Cloud EKM lets the external key manager control a project's permission to use its external key. Revoking that permission stops subsequent cryptographic requests.

cards.statement: Secret Manager can replace an existing secret version's payload when an application rotates its credentials.
cards.explanation: Secret Manager keeps a version's payload immutable. A rotated credential belongs in a new version, preserving the value referenced by existing version-specific consumers.
cards.misconception: Rotating a credential replaces the payload of its existing secret version.

cards.statement: VPC Service Controls restricts protected API access from unauthorized networks despite permissive IAM grants.
cards.explanation: VPC Service Controls enforces service-perimeter access independently of IAM. Its network restrictions provide another boundary when an IAM policy exposes protected data.

cards.statement: Identity-Aware Proxy can apply Access Context Manager access levels, such as device or IP conditions, to app users.
cards.explanation: IAP attaches access levels to the IAM grants of an IAP-secured app, so users get in only from approved IP ranges or trusted devices; device attributes need a Chrome Enterprise Premium license.

source.title: Setting up context-aware access with Identity-Aware Proxy

cards.statement: Workload Identity Federation limits resource-access IAM grants to service accounts that workloads impersonate.
cards.explanation: Workload Identity Federation supports IAM grants to identities in a workload identity pool. Service account impersonation is an alternative for resources or APIs that need it.
cards.misconception: IAM grants for federated workloads target impersonated service accounts rather than external identities.

cards.statement: Model Armor uses Sensitive Data Protection to screen sensitive data in prompts and model responses.
cards.explanation: Model Armor integrates Sensitive Data Protection inspection with its prompt and response screening. That gives an AI application a data-leakage check on both sides of a model interaction.
cards.volatilityNote: Model Armor's filter integrations and screening capabilities continue to evolve.

cards.statement: Assured Workloads scopes a control package to a folder and the projects and resources beneath it.
cards.explanation: An Assured Workloads folder defines the workload's compliance boundary. Its selected control package sets guardrails for projects and resources inside that folder.

cards.statement: Access Transparency lets a customer approve Google personnel access before engineers read customer data.
cards.explanation: Access Transparency records Google personnel's actions when they access customer data. Access Approval provides the customer authorization step for covered access requests.
cards.misconception: Access Transparency requires customer approval before Google personnel access data.

cards.statement: Sensitive Data Protection can tokenize legacy IDs while preserving their length and character set.
cards.explanation: Sensitive Data Protection's format preserving encryption keeps the encrypted value's length and character set, which helps retain compatibility with legacy field schemas.

cards.statement: Key Access Justifications lets a key policy deny a Cloud KMS request by its justification code.
cards.explanation: Beyond logging why a key is used, Key Access Justifications policies can approve or deny key access per justification code; this depends on the Assured Workloads control package chosen.

cards.statement: Cloud Logging automatically stores a project's Admin Activity and System Event audit logs in its _Required bucket.
cards.explanation: Cloud Logging keeps Admin Activity and System Event audit logs in the generating project's _Required bucket. Routing copies elsewhere preserves that local audit record.

cards.statement: BigQuery treats Data Access audit logging as an opt-in feature for newly created projects.
cards.explanation: BigQuery generates Data Access audit logs by default. An architect planning an audit trail can rely on this service-specific default rather than an initial opt-in step.
cards.misconception: BigQuery requires an initial opt-in to generate Data Access audit logs.

cards.statement: Cloud Logging automatically blocks deletion of a project containing a retention-locked log bucket.
cards.explanation: Cloud Logging's retention lock leaves project deletion available. Add a project lien separately to protect the containing project and its audit logs against accidental deletion.
cards.misconception: A log bucket retention lock also prevents deletion of its containing project.

cards.statement: Organization Policy Service can suspend existing resources outside a new allowed-location policy.
cards.explanation: The resource locations constraint applies to new resource creation. Resources created before the policy remain in place and continue operating, so existing violations need separate remediation.
cards.misconception: A newly enforced resource location constraint suspends previously deployed resources outside the allowed locations.

cards.statement: Signing Google's HIPAA BAA transfers evaluation of the customer's application compliance to Google.
cards.explanation: Google's BAA supports HIPAA compliance, while the customer evaluates its own compliance and secures its environment and applications.
cards.misconception: Google takes over evaluating the customer's application compliance after signing the HIPAA BAA.

source.title: HIPAA compliance on Google Cloud and Google Workspace

cards.statement: Cloud Build private pool workers can run inside the customer's VPC network used for private access.
cards.explanation: Cloud Build hosts private pool workers in a Google-owned service producer network. A peering connection gives those workers access to the customer's private resources.
cards.misconception: Private access places private pool workers inside the customer's VPC network.

cards.statement: Artifact Registry cleanup policies can delete an artifact matching both a keep policy and a delete policy.
cards.explanation: Artifact Registry keeps artifacts that match both a cleanup keep policy and a delete policy. Keep-policy precedence protects designated artifacts from broader cleanup rules.
cards.misconception: A matching delete policy takes precedence over a cleanup keep policy.

cards.statement: Cloud Deploy carries a staging rollout's approval forward to a production target that requires approval.
cards.explanation: Cloud Deploy approvals authorize a rollout to a specific target. A later rollout into an approval-protected production target needs its own approval.
cards.misconception: Approval of a release in staging authorizes its later production rollout.

source.title: Promote your release and manage approvals

cards.statement: Teams select a Secure Source Manager instance's region to control where that instance hosts repositories.
cards.explanation: Secure Source Manager hosts repositories within a regionally deployed instance. Architects select the instance's region when repository placement is a requirement.

cards.statement: Infrastructure Manager previews cover first-time deployments as well as updates to existing deployments.
cards.explanation: An Infrastructure Manager preview runs Terraform plan for a new deployment or an update, so the team reviews the resources planned for provisioning before anything is created.

cards.statement: Service Catalog stores a user's Terraform deployment state in the catalog administrator's project.
cards.explanation: Service Catalog's Terraform deployment state is created and stored in the project where the user deploys the configuration. Sharing the configuration leaves that state in the consuming project.
cards.misconception: Shared Terraform solutions centralize consuming users' deployment state in the catalog project.

cards.statement: Google lists an on-call intervention, such as a release rollback, among the triggers for a postmortem.
cards.explanation: Google's postmortem criteria include on-call interventions such as a release rollback or rerouted traffic, alongside user-visible downtime, data loss of any kind and monitoring failures.

cards.statement: Google recommends restoring backups into production, where real dependencies run, when testing that they are usable.
cards.explanation: Google recommends restoring backups in a non-production environment and testing the entire application stack and critical infrastructure services with the restored data.
cards.misconception: Restoring backups into production is the recommended way to prove they are usable.

source.title: Perform testing for recovery from data loss

cards.statement: Google recommends granting users in the DR environment the access they hold in production.
cards.explanation: Users must be able to work in the recovered environment; when production runs on Google Cloud, IaC tools such as Terraform can replicate its IAM policies in the DR environment.

cards.statement: The Well-Architected Framework says sole-tenant node costs can qualify as capital expenditure.
cards.explanation: The cost pillar lists Compute Engine sole-tenant nodes as a service whose costs might receive capital-expenditure treatment.
cards.volatilityNote: Accounting guidance for sole-tenant node payments can change.

cards.statement: Compute Engine's idle VM recommender can treat low CPU usage as sufficient evidence of inactivity.
cards.explanation: Compute Engine evaluates CPU and network activity when identifying idle VMs. Low CPU usage alone leaves the network evidence unaccounted for.
cards.misconception: The idle VM recommender treats low CPU utilization as sufficient to establish inactivity.

cards.statement: Compute Engine bases machine type recommendations on peak CPU utilization rather than sampled averages.
cards.explanation: Compute Engine uses averaged CPU metrics for machine type recommendations. Short bursts can be missed, so a recommended smaller VM may lack needed burst capacity.
cards.misconception: Machine type recommendations capture peak CPU demand rather than relying on interval averages.

source.title: Apply machine type recommendations to VM instances

cards.statement: Cloud Billing's detailed usage cost export can directly attribute Compute Engine charges to individual VM resources.
cards.explanation: The detailed Cloud Billing export adds resource-level cost data. Teams use the VM identity in eligible usage records to investigate which instance drives spending.

source.title: Export Cloud Billing data to BigQuery

cards.statement: Cloud Billing groups late-reported usage into the invoice for the month in which that usage occurs.
cards.explanation: Late-reported Cloud Billing usage can appear on a later invoice. Invoice-month data is the basis for invoice reconciliation, while usage timestamps track when consumption occurs.
cards.misconception: The usage month and invoice month coincide for late-reported usage.

cards.statement: Cloud Billing exports show a new label's costs only from the date the label was applied to a resource.
cards.explanation: Labels aren't retroactive: the export shows a label's costs from the date it was applied, so apply labels before the period you need to allocate.

cards.statement: Unused commitment from one hour of a standard spend-based CUD carries over to cover usage in a later hour.
cards.explanation: Standard spend-based CUDs apply hourly: if eligible usage in an hour falls below the commitment you still pay the full amount, and the unused part doesn't roll over. Flexible Savings Plans use a monthly window.
cards.misconception: Unused spend-based commitment banks credit for later hours.

cards.statement: Cloud Billing sizes its CUD recommendations from an organization's expected future usage growth.
cards.explanation: CUD recommendations come from historical and recent usage, including usage already covered by commitments, so architects weigh planned growth or decline themselves.
cards.misconception: CUD recommendations are sized from forecast business growth.

source.title: Get recommendations for committed use discounts (CUDs)

cards.statement: GKE cost allocation must be enabled on a Standard cluster before billing exports show its namespace costs.
cards.explanation: Once GKE cost allocation is enabled, the detailed Cloud Billing export to BigQuery carries cluster, namespace and workload labels for chargeback; otherwise those costs carry no GKE labels.

source.title: Get key spending insights for your GKE resource allocation and cluster costs

cards.statement: Migrate to Virtual Machines can create a test clone for validation while the source workload stays live.
cards.explanation: Migrate to Virtual Machines builds a test clone from replicated data. A team validates that separate clone while the source continues serving traffic.

cards.statement: Apigee's Quota policy can pace an application's permitted API calls evenly over the quota measurement interval.
cards.explanation: Apigee's Quota policy counts requests over its configured interval. A client can consume its allowance in a burst; SpikeArrest handles traffic-spike protection.
cards.misconception: A request quota spaces an application's allowed calls evenly through the quota period.

cards.statement: Apigee hybrid processes API traffic in the runtime plane hosted in a customer-managed Kubernetes cluster.
cards.explanation: Apigee hybrid's runtime services handle API calls in the customer's Kubernetes environment. That runtime boundary keeps API traffic processing under the customer's network control.

cards.statement: Migrate to Virtual Machines supports Google Cloud VMware Engine as the destination for on-premises vSphere VMs.
cards.explanation: Migrate to Virtual Machines accepts Google Cloud VMware Engine as a source and moves VM workloads into Compute Engine. VMware Engine is a source platform in this migration path.
cards.misconception: Migrate to Virtual Machines targets VMware Engine rather than Compute Engine for on-premises vSphere migrations.

cards.statement: Google recommends continuing PostgreSQL source writes while promoting a continuous Database Migration Service job.
cards.explanation: Google's PostgreSQL migration guidance stops source writes and waits for replication lag to reach zero before promotion. This makes the destination the primary database at cutover.
cards.misconception: A continuous database migration preserves source writes through destination promotion.

source.title: Migrate a database to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL by using Database Migration Service

cards.statement: Storage Transfer Service's checksum validation confirms that a copied file is the latest version at the source.
cards.explanation: Storage Transfer Service validates transferred data using available checksums. Google recommends separate checks for the correct file version when files change at the source.
cards.misconception: A successful transfer checksum proves that the destination holds the latest source version.

cards.statement: Transfer Appliance keeps EU customers' offline data transfers within the EU when they choose an EU destination region.
cards.explanation: Google handles EU customers' Transfer Appliance shipping and data upload through Belgium. An EU destination region keeps the transfer process within EU boundaries.
cards.volatilityNote: Transfer Appliance logistics and regional processing arrangements can change.

cards.statement: Datastream delivers change events into Cloud Storage in source commit order.
cards.explanation: Datastream delivers change events that can arrive out of order. A Cloud Storage consumer uses source-specific event metadata to reconstruct the source operation order.
cards.misconception: Datastream guarantees source commit order in the sequence of delivered change events.

cards.statement: Gemini Cloud Assist can refine Terraform code through conversations about a team's infrastructure requirements.
cards.explanation: Gemini Cloud Assist iteratively generates or refines Terraform through interactive infrastructure discussions. Google recommends validating its generated output before use.
cards.volatilityNote: Gemini Cloud Assist is a Preview offering whose infrastructure assistance can change.

cards.statement: Google recommends attached service account credentials for Application Default Credentials in Google Cloud production.
cards.explanation: Google's production guidance favors the service account attached to the compute resource. The application obtains credentials from its environment rather than carrying a key file.

cards.statement: Application Default Credentials prioritizes an attached service account over a credential file set in the environment.
cards.explanation: Application Default Credentials checks the environment-specified credential file before the attached service account. A file left in the environment can change which identity a deployed workload uses.
cards.misconception: An attached service account takes precedence over an environment-specified credential file.

cards.statement: The Spanner emulator enforces IAM permissions on requests that an application's integration tests send to it.
cards.explanation: The Spanner emulator supports no authentication, IAM, permissions or roles, so access grants still need testing against a real Spanner instance.
cards.misconception: The Spanner emulator reproduces production IAM enforcement for tests.

cards.statement: Retrying Cloud Storage's Pub/Sub notification creation after a timeout can create duplicate configurations.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage creates a fresh notification ID on each successful creation request. A timeout can hide a successful first attempt, so retrying that call can add another configuration.

cards.statement: The Bigtable emulator writes test data to local disk so a later emulator process can reuse it.
cards.explanation: The Bigtable emulator keeps its data in memory and loses it across runs. Tests that need an initial dataset populate that dataset for a new emulator run.
cards.misconception: The Bigtable emulator persists application data on local disk between processes.

cards.statement: Google API Client Libraries can use gRPC for an integration with an API that offers REST and gRPC.
cards.explanation: Google API Client Libraries expose REST. An integration that needs gRPC uses a gRPC-capable Cloud Client Library or a generated gRPC client instead.
cards.misconception: Google API Client Libraries provide gRPC transport when the API exposes it.

source.title: Client libraries and Cloud APIs explained

cards.statement: Infrastructure Manager keeps a Terraform state file per deployment and per revision.
cards.explanation: Infrastructure Manager creates a Terraform state file per deployment and per revision; a team can download a state file to inspect or modify it.

cards.statement: Config Connector corrects drift in declared readable, mutable fields through periodic reconciliation by default.
cards.explanation: Config Connector treats the declared configuration as the desired state. Later reconciliations can overwrite direct changes to readable, mutable fields, so external edits can compete with it.

cards.statement: Cloud Shell's VM automatically joins the selected project's VPC network for private resource access.
cards.explanation: Google hosts the Cloud Shell VM outside the customer's VPC network. Selecting a project leaves that network boundary in place, so private IP access needs a separate connectivity path.
cards.misconception: Selecting a project places the Cloud Shell VM in that project's VPC network.

cards.statement: Google's example error budget policy allows routine feature releases while a service exceeds its error budget.
cards.explanation: Google's example error budget policy halts routine changes after the service exceeds its budget. Critical incident and security fixes are exceptions while the team restores SLO compliance.
cards.misconception: An exhausted error budget leaves routine feature releases proceeding as usual.

cards.statement: Cloud Monitoring can warn of rapid SLO error-budget consumption while the service still has budget remaining.
cards.explanation: Cloud Monitoring burn-rate alerts evaluate the rate of error-budget consumption. A fast-burn alert warns of sustained errors that would soon exhaust the budget, giving operators time to respond.

cards.statement: To export logs received before a sink existed, Cloud Logging offers a copy from the log bucket to Cloud Storage.
cards.explanation: Sinks route only entries that arrive after they're created; for entries already stored in a log bucket, Cloud Logging can copy them retroactively to Cloud Storage.

cards.statement: BigQuery lets analysts update log entries through a dataset linked to a Cloud Logging bucket.
cards.explanation: A linked BigQuery dataset gives read access to log data stored by Cloud Logging. Analysts query that data through BigQuery, while the linked dataset leaves the original log entries unchanged.
cards.misconception: Linking a log bucket to BigQuery enables analysts to modify the source log entries.

source.title: Create a linked BigQuery dataset on a log bucket

cards.statement: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus answers a PromQL query from a single Google Cloud region's data.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus evaluates queries against a global datastore and combines results across regions. Teams obtain a unified view rather than querying isolated regional servers.
cards.misconception: Managed Prometheus query evaluation is confined to one regional datastore.
tags: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus

source.title: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus

cards.statement: Cloud Trace can directly apply tail-based sampling to incoming spans using a completed request's latency.
cards.explanation: Cloud Trace receives spans selected by sending components. Tail-based selection needs an upstream component, such as an OpenTelemetry Collector, to choose which spans to send.
cards.misconception: Cloud Trace performs tail-based selection after receiving the completed trace.

cards.statement: Cloud Profiler can collect profiles from applications that run outside Google Cloud, such as on premises.
cards.explanation: Cloud Profiler agents for Go, Java, Node.js and Python also run outside Google Cloud, so hybrid workloads can send low-overhead profiles to a Google Cloud project; profile types vary by language.

cards.statement: Cloud Monitoring can run private uptime checks against a VPC in a project outside its metrics scope.
cards.explanation: For private uptime checks, the Service Directory service belongs in the metrics scope. The VPC and resources represented by that service may reside in another project outside the scope.

cards.statement: Cloud Monitoring retains elapsed retest time when a metric-threshold alert condition briefly clears.
cards.explanation: For Cloud Monitoring metric-threshold alerts, a nonviolating measurement resets the retest window. A brief recovery restarts the wait rather than preserving the elapsed violation time.
cards.misconception: Separate threshold-violation bursts accumulate toward one retest window.

cards.statement: Cloud Deploy advances canary phases across regional targets through their shared controller rollout.
cards.explanation: A Cloud Deploy multi-target rollout advances its child rollouts when the controller advances. This coordinates progressive deployment across regional targets.

cards.statement: Setting maxUnavailable to 0 in a MIG rolling update removes the need for spare quota during the update.
cards.explanation: With maxUnavailable at 0 and maxSurge above 0, the MIG creates each replacement VM before deleting the old one, and maxSurge only works when there is quota and capacity for the extra VMs.
cards.misconception: A rolling update with zero unavailable VMs needs no extra quota.

source.title: Automatically apply VM configuration updates in a MIG

cards.statement: Cloud Run resets a service's traffic split to the latest revision by default after another deployment.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run preserves an existing traffic split pattern across subsequent deployments. A team changes the traffic allocation explicitly to return traffic to the latest revision.
cards.misconception: Another deployment clears an existing traffic split and restores the latest revision as the sole traffic destination.

source.title: Rollbacks, gradual rollouts, and traffic migration

cards.statement: By default, a Cloud Deploy rollback redeploys the last release that had a successful rollout to that target.
cards.explanation: Cloud Deploy creates a new rollout from the last release that succeeded on the target unless the team picks another release; it does not rewind the earlier rollout.

cards.statement: Cloud Deploy automatically marks a rollout as failed when post-deployment verification reports failure.
cards.explanation: Cloud Deploy runs the team's verification tests after deployment. Failed verification fails the rollout, giving the team a quality gate before treating that delivery as successful.

cards.statement: In Google's incident response model, the Ops Lead takes on any incident role that remains undelegated.
cards.explanation: The SRE Workbook says the Incident Commander assumes every role not yet delegated, including Ops Lead; delegating them lets the IC focus on coordination and communication.
cards.misconception: The Ops Lead absorbs incident roles that nobody has been assigned.

cards.statement: Google recommends combining failure simulations with load testing to assess behavior during real usage.
cards.explanation: Google's recovery testing guidance adds realistic request load to simulated outages. This tests how the system behaves when failures happen while users are active.

source.title: Perform testing for recovery from failures

cards.statement: Google Cloud requires notification before penetration testing that affects just a customer's own projects.
cards.explanation: Google permits penetration testing of a customer's projects without prior contact. The tester follows the Acceptable Use Policy and Terms of Service and confines effects to their own projects.
cards.misconception: A tester needs to notify Google before a penetration test limited to the tester's own projects.

cards.statement: Google recommends isolating a Spanner load test from other services when validating production peak capacity.
cards.explanation: Google's Spanner launch checklist includes interacting services and realistic user journeys in load tests. Isolated database tests miss competing application and background workloads.
cards.misconception: An isolated database benchmark is Google's recommended way to validate peak capacity for a production Spanner application.
